'''''Fumaria officinalis''''', the '''common fumitory''', '''drug fumitory''' or '''earth smoke''', is a herbaceous annual [[flowering plant]] in the poppy family [[Papaveraceae]]. It is the most common species of the genus ''[[Fumaria]]'' in [[Western Europe|Western]] and [[Central Europe]].

==Description==
It is an [[herbaceous]] [[annual plant]] that grows weakly erect and scrambling, with stalks about {{convert|10|-|50|cm|abbr=on}} long. It has slender green leaves.<ref name="Reader's Digest-1981"/> Its pink {{convert|7|-|9|mm|abbr=on}} flowers appear from April to October in the northern hemisphere,<ref name="Fitter-1974"/> or May to September in the UK.<ref name="Reader's Digest-1981">{{cite book |year=1981 |title=Reader's Digest Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain |page=37 |publisher=[[Reader's Digest]] |isbn=9780276002175}}</ref> They are two lipped and spurred, with [[sepal]]s running a quarter the length of the petals.<ref name="Fitter-1974">{{cite book | last1 = Fitter | first1 = Richard | last2 = Fitter | first2 = Alastair | last3 = Blamey | first3 = Marjorie | title = The Wild Flowers of Britain and Northern Europe | publisher = Collins | year = 1974 | location = London | pages = 78 | isbn = 0-00-219057-5}}<!--| accessdate = 2011-05-14 --></ref> The plant commonly has more than 20 and up to 60 flowers per spike.<ref name="Murphy-2009">{{cite book|first=R.J.|last=Murphy|title=Fumitories of Britain and Ireland. BSBI Handbbok No. 12|date=2009|publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland|location=London|isbn=9780901158406}}</ref> The fruit is an [[achene]] containing one seed. It is approximately globular, slightly wider than high and with an apical notch.<ref name="Murphy-2009"/> It contains [[alkaloid]]s, [[potassium salt]]s, and [[tannin]]s and is also a source of [[fumaric acid]].<ref name="Chinou-2011">{{cite report |author=Ioanna Chinou |date=13 September 2011 |title=Assessment report on Fumaria officinalis L., herba |url=https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/herbal-report/final-assessment-report-fumaria-officinalis-l-herba_en.pdf |publisher=European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) |docket=EMA/HMPC/576232/2010 |access-date=5 May 2019}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
It was first formally described by the Swedish botanist [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his seminal publication '[[Species Plantarum]]' on page 700, in 1753.<ref name="plantlist">{{cite web|title=Fumaria officinalis L. is an accepted name|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2815499|date=23 March 2012|publisher=theplantlist.org|access-date=5 November 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Papaveraceae Fumaria officinalis L.|url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=673050-1|publisher=ipni.org|access-date=5 November 2017}}</ref>

There are 2 known subspecies:
* ''Fumaria officinalis'' subsp. ''cilicica'' <small>(Hausskn.) Lidén</small>
* ''Fumaria officinalis'' subsp. ''wirtgenii'' <small>(Koch) Arcang.</small><ref name="plantlist"/>

==Etymology==
[[File:(MHNT) Fumaria officinalis - Plant habit.jpg|thumb|Flower and leaves of ''Fumaria officinalis'']]
The "smoky" or "fumy" origin of its name comes from the translucent color of its flowers, giving them the appearance of smoke or of hanging in smoke, and the slightly gray-blue haze color of its foliage, also resembling smoke coming from the ground, especially after morning dew.{{citation required|date=December 2023}}

The plant was already called ''{{lang|la|fūmus terrae}}'' (smoke of the earth) in the early 13th century, and two thousand years ago, [[Dioscorides]] wrote in ''{{lang|la|De Materia Medica}}'' ({{lang|grc|Περὶ ὕλης ἰατρικῆς}}) and [[Pliny the Elder]] in ''{{lang|la|[[Natural History (Pliny)|Naturalis Historia]]}}'' that rubbing the eyes with the sap or latex of the plant causes tears, like acrid smoke (''{{lang|la|fūmus}}'') does to the eyes.
Its Greek name is ''kapnos'' (''{{lang|grc|καπνός}}'', for ''smoke'') and the name ''fumewort'' now applies mostly to the genus ''[[Corydalis]]'', especially the similar looking ''[[Corydalis solida]]'' (formerly ''Fumaria bulbosa''), which was thought to belong to the same genus as fumitory.<ref name="Gledhill-2008">[https://books.google.com/books?id=NJ6PyhVuecwC&dq=fumus+terrae&pg=PA172 The Names of Plants, Fourth Edition], {{cite book | last1 = Gledhill | first1 = D. |title = The Names of Plants | url = https://archive.org/details/namesofplants00gled | url-access = registration | publisher = Cambridge University Press | year = 1985–2008 | location = United Kingdom | pages = 443 | isbn = 978-0-521-86645-3}}<!--| accessdate = 2014-04-13 --></ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
It is [[native plant|native]] to temperate regions of North Africa, Europe and parts of Western Asia.<ref name="GRIN">{{cite web |title=Taxon: Fumaria officinalis L. |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=70905 |publisher=ars-grin.gov |access-date=5 November 2017}}</ref>

===Range===
It is found in North Africa, within [[Macaronesia]], [[Canary Islands]], [[Algeria]], [[Egypt]], [[Libya]], [[Morocco]] and [[Tunisia]]. Within Western Asia it is found in the [[Caucasus]], [[Cyprus]], [[Iraq]], [[Israel]], [[Lebanon]], [[Siberia]], [[Syria]] and [[Turkey]]. In eastern Europe, it is found within [[Belarus]], [[Estonia]], [[Latvia]], [[Lithuania]] and [[Ukraine]]. In middle Europe, it is in [[Austria]], [[Belgium]], [[Germany]], [[Hungary]], [[Netherlands]], [[Poland]], [[Slovakia]] and [[Switzerland]]. In northern Europe, in [[Denmark]], [[Ireland]], [[Norway]], [[Sweden]] and [[United Kingdom]]. In southeastern Europe, within [[Albania]], [[Bosnia and Herzegovina]], [[Bulgaria]], [[Croatia]], [[Greece]], [[Italy]], [[Montenegro]], [[North Macedonia]], [[Romania]], [[Serbia]] and [[Slovenia]]. Also in southwestern Europe, it is found in [[France]], [[Portugal]] and [[Spain]].<ref name="GRIN"/> It is common in Australia where it was introduced.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://bie.ala.org.au/species/https://id.biodiversity.org.au/node/apni/2904208 |title=Fumaria officinalis L. /Common Fumitory |work=Atlas Of Living Australia |access-date=2024-07-09}}</ref>

==Herbalism==
[[File:Storage jar used for Fumitory Water, Italy, 1640-1660 Wellcome L0057089.jpg|thumb|Storage jar used for fumitory water (water infused with ''Fumaria officinalis''), Italy, mid-17th century]]
Usage of this plant as medicine began in Europe in the late Middle Ages, although it was known since antiquity.<ref name="Chinou-2011"/> In 17th century Europe it was publicised as good for the eyes (due to remarks by [[Pliny the Elder|Pliny]] and later [[Olivier de Serres]] that rubbing its juice in one's eyes caused excessive tearing).<ref name="Chinou-2011"/><ref name="Howard-1987">Howard, Michael. ''Traditional Folk Remedies'' (century, 1987). pp142-3. {{ISBN|9780712617314}}</ref> The most common traditional uses were as a digestive aid and a [[diuretic]], but various folk traditions throughout Europe ascribed to it a multitude of uses: constipation, [[cystitis]], [[arteriosclerosis]], [[rheumatism]], [[arthritis]], as a blood purifier, for [[hypoglycaemia]], infections,<ref name="Chinou-2011"/> and possibly to cleanse the kidneys.<ref name="Howard-1987"/> In [[Sicily]] and perhaps elsewhere it was used to treat [[Skin condition|skin blemishes]], and in [[United Kingdom|Britain]] into the modern era as an eyewash to treat [[conjunctivitis]].<ref name="Chinou-2011"/><ref name="Howard-1987"/><ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Amenta R, Camarda L, Di Stefano V, Lentini F, Venza F|title=Traditional medicine as a source of new therapeutic agents against psoriasis|journal=Fitoterapia|volume=71 Suppl 1 |pages=S13–20 |year=2000 |pmid=10930708 |doi=10.1016/s0367-326x(00)00172-6 }}</ref>

Since 1963, it has been marketed as a herbal medicine in [[France]].<ref name="Chinou-2011"/> As of 2011, herbal products made from this plant are legally sold in various forms in [[Austria]], [[Germany]], France and [[Spain]]. Products may be legally sold in the British market (it is on the British [[General Sales List]]), although no products were sold there as of 2011. In the European Union as a whole, marketing of the plant is not necessarily legal: it has been rejected from the Community List by the [[Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products]] due to the lack of toxicology studies. Products in France and Spain are marketed as a digestive (said to work by increasing bile flow), in Austria it is sold for treatment of [[dyskinesia]] of the [[biliary duct]], in Germany it is simply sold as an herbal tea.<ref name="Chinou-2011"/>

There is some evidence from animal models that it modifies abnormal bile flow, although it has no effect on normal [[choleresis]]. An [[antispasmodic]] effect on the upper digestive tract [[in vitro]] and in animal studies is considered sufficiently documented. The efficacy of the herbal products in humans is considered plausible but yet unproven in clinical studies. Numerous clinical studies in its amphocholeretic uses in humans have demonstrated the tolerability and safety of dosages used, but there has only been one small double-blind trial with placebos which was inconclusive regarding efficacy. A larger double-blind trial with [[placebo]]s investigating and comparing its use in the treatment of pain and distension due to [[irritable bowel syndrome]] with [[Turmeric|''Curcuma'']] demonstrated no statistically significant differences between treatment groups (although use of either herb appeared to slightly worsen either distension or pain respectively, compared to placebo use). A number of other potential effects or uses for the plant and its major alkaloid [[protopine]] have been researched in vitro or in animal models.<ref name="Chinou-2011"/>

Howard (1987) warns that fumitory is [[poison]]ous and should only be used "under the direction of a medical herbalist",<ref name="Howard-1987"/> but in Europe, no safety problems with its use have been recorded as of 2011.<ref name="Chinou-2011"/> Large doses of protopine in animal models causes excitation and convulsions. Thorough toxicological research on this plant has not been conducted as of 2011. There have been no studies on its safety or effect on pregnant woman, children or elderly.<ref name="Chinou-2011"/>

==Chemical constituents==
[[File:Protopine Structural Formula V1.svg|thumb|left|200px|Protopine]]
[[File:Illustration Fumaria officinalis0.jpg|thumb|left|200px|''Fumaria officinalis'']]
The plant contains [[isoquinoline]] alkaloids [[protopine]] and [[allocryptopine]]. Both protopine and allocryptopine increased [[CYP1A1]] and [[CYP1A2]] [[mRNA]] levels in human [[hepatocyte]] cells. The use of products containing protopine and/or allocryptopine may be considered safe in terms of possible induction of [[CYP1A]] enzymes.<ref>{{Cite journal
